summary:
Vichada stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed legal regimes for trans people in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the government official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

That framework coexists with lethal violence against trans people across the country. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed, the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon after drowning in a creek with fractured limbs. Police questioned local residents and, even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, no arrest had been reported. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed actors. In Caquetá department, groups have run a "social cleansing" campaign whose flyers and WhatsApp messages name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; a trans woman standing as a local election candidate was given one week by three armed men to leave town and fled at night, and trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats. In Guajira, armed groups have circulated kill lists of named individuals since March 2024. Discrimination confines many trans women in these departments to hairdressing or sex work, and eight trans women were killed nationwide between February and April 2024. The material assembled for this record contains no documented trans-specific incident within Vichada itself; the finding carried to the department is the national pattern of daylight, filmed killings and organised threats in which arrests are rare.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising and widespread discrimination requiring urgent attention.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to premises and to custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at the Cosmocentro mall in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
The violence documented in the sources is concentrated in departments where armed groups exercise territorial control, notably Caquetá and Guajira, and persists amid Colombia's decades-long civil conflict; reporting on the Millerey case characterised the brutality as calculated rather than incidental. Vichada sits within the same national conflict geography, but the inventory supplies no assessment of armed-group presence or of threat levels specific to the department.

Institutional reform and lived experience diverge sharply. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission praised the legal architecture while recording widespread discrimination and rising killings, and the Attorney General's figures for 2025 show LGBTI homicides continuing after the Millerey case. A visitor should read the statutory protections as real but unevenly enforced, with arrest and prosecution rates for trans-phobic killings low even when the head of state orders an investigation.

Trans women's economic marginalisation is part of the risk surface: in the affected departments discrimination limits them mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which raises exposure to armed actors, to police attention and to displacement. Two documented trans women were forced from their homes by threat, one given a week to leave town and another moving twice.
localsOnly:
Resident trans Colombians obtain a marker change on identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015; the same offices are the ones ordered by the National Registry memo to register same-sex marriages performed abroad. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 underpins recognition on the basis of self-recognition alone, and identity documents issued from November 2025 carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers.

Domestic protections run through the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree, which obliges government institutions on LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and in the treatment of victims of armed conflict, and the May 2018 executive decree extending guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Prisoners have a Constitutional Court ruling confirming the right to choose hairstyle and makeup, and a further court ruling addresses the treatment of trans detainees.

Entry to public and commercial premises is protected by Constitutional Court judgments concerning a Cali shopping mall, a Santa Marta boardwalk and the Tequendama Hotel, which bind police and private security. Same-sex couples married abroad hold the same inheritance, pension and healthcare entitlements as other spouses.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a trans-specific incident, arrest, prosecution or protection measure within Vichada department itself; the violence findings are national or drawn from other departments and are carried to Vichada as pattern evidence only.

The inventory does not resolve how the November 2025 introduction of "trans" and "non-binary" markers is being implemented at registry offices in Vichada, nor whether notary-based marker changes are available without travel to the departmental capital. Local facility availability, hospital practice on gender-affirming care, and police responsiveness in Vichada are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

Whether armed groups named in the Caquetá and Guajira material operate within Vichada is not addressed by any source provided; the conflict-adjacency of the department is therefore an open question rather than a sourced finding. The count of 41 trans women killed in 2023 and 8 between February and April 2024 comes from reporting rather than a single official register, and the two figures may rest on different counting methods.
